PhenoRec Tutorial: Phenotype-Preserving Integration of scRNA-seq Data

In this tutorial, we demonstrate how to use PhenoRec for the phenotype-preserving integration of scRNA-seq data. We use a publicly available type 1 diabetes (T1D) dataset download from the CZ CELLxGENE Data Portal.

The T1D dataset was obtained from the study by Fasolino et al., which profiled human pancreatic islets. Donors were classified into three phenotype groups: healthy controls, autoantibody positive individuals without a clinical diagnosis of T1D (AAB+), and individuals with T1D. The dataset comprised 65,220 cells from 11 control, 8 AAB+, and 5 T1D donors.

The analysis consists of four main stages:

  1. Preprocess the scRNA-seq data.
  2. Estimate latent cell states.
  3. Apply PhenoRec to recover phenotype-associated signals.
  4. Visualize the phenotype-preserving integrated data.

1 Load required packages

We first load packages required for running this tutorial.

library(PhenoRec)
library(Seurat)
library(anndata)
library(ggplot2)
library(Matrix)
library(dplyr)

2 Load data

For this example, the T1D dataset is stored in AnnData format (.h5ad). We use the anndata package to read the dataset into R.

data <- read_h5ad("T1D.h5ad")
data

The AnnData object contains two components used in this tutorial:

  • data$X: the cell-by-gene expression matrix.
  • data$obs: cell-level metadata.

We extract these components.

metadata <- data$obs
data_matrix <- data$X

3 Prepare cell metadata

PhenoRec requires two types of metadata as input:

  • a batch label.
  • a phenotype label.

In this dataset, donor_id identifies batch/sample and disease_state represents the phenotype of interest.

We convert both variables to character format.

metadata$donor_id <- as.character(metadata$donor_id)
metadata$disease_state <- as.character(metadata$disease_state)

For visualization, we also simplify the original cell-type annotations.

map <- c(
  "pancreatic A cell" = "Alpha cells",
  "type B pancreatic cell" = "Beta cells",
  "endothelial cell" = "Endothelial cells",
  "pancreatic D cell" = "Delta cells",
  "pancreatic stellate cell" = "Stellate cells",
  "pancreatic ductal cell" = "Ductal cells",
  "unknown" = "unknown",
  "pancreatic acinar cell" = "Acinar cells",
  "pancreatic epsilon cell" = "Epsilon cells",
  "PP cell" = "PP cells"
)

metadata$cell_type_rename <- map[as.character(metadata$cell_type)]

4 Preprocess the scRNA-seq data using Seurat

We next construct a Seurat object from the expression matrix and metadata.

seurat_data <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = t(data_matrix),
  assay = "RNA",
  meta.data = metadata
)
## Warning: Data is of class dgRMatrix. Coercing to dgCMatrix.

The input matrix to CreateSeuratObject() is expected to have genes as rows and cells as columns, so the cell-by-gene matrix is transposed.

Cells without a defined cell-type annotation are excluded from this example.

seurat_data <- subset(
  seurat_data,
  subset = cell_type_rename != "unknown"
)

We then perform the preprocessing steps following the Seurat workflow. If you are unfamiliar with this workflow, please refer to their official tutorial.

seurat_data <- FindVariableFeatures(
  seurat_data,
  nfeatures = 3000
)
## Finding variable features for layer counts
seurat_data <- NormalizeData(seurat_data)
## Normalizing layer: counts
seurat_data@assays$RNA$data <-
  t(data_matrix[colnames(seurat_data), ])

seurat_data <- ScaleData(seurat_data)
## Centering and scaling data matrix
## Warning in asMethod(object): sparse->dense coercion: allocating vector of size
## 1.5 GiB
seurat_data <- RunPCA(
  seurat_data,
  features = VariableFeatures(seurat_data),
  npcs = 200
)

5 Visualization of the unintegrated data

Before performing integration, it is useful to visualize the unintegrated dataset.

We construct a UMAP based on the first 50 principal components.

seurat_data <- RunUMAP(
  seurat_data,
  dims = 1:50
)
## Warning: The default method for RunUMAP has changed from calling Python UMAP via reticulate to the R-native UWOT using the cosine metric

We visualize the embedding using three annotations:

  • cell type;
  • batch/sample identity;
  • phenotype.
DimPlot(
  seurat_data,
  group.by = "cell_type_rename"
) +
  DimPlot(
    seurat_data,
    group.by = "donor_id"
  ) +
  DimPlot(
    seurat_data,
    group.by = "disease_state"
  )

These three views serve different purposes.

The cell-type plot shows the cell-state structure of the dataset.

The donor plot reveals sample-specific variation. This plot reveals substantial sample-specific batch effects, with cells from the same sample tending to cluster together and clear separation between samples.

The phenotype plot shows biological variation associated with disease state.

6 Estimate latent cell states using Harmony

PhenoRec first requires an estimate of the underlying cell-state representation, denoted conceptually by (Z).

In the current implementation, we obtain this representation using Harmony.

harmony_z <- harmony::RunHarmony(
  seurat_data@reductions$pca@cell.embeddings,
  seurat_data@meta.data,
  "donor_id"
)
## Transposing data matrix
## Initializing state using k-means centroids initialization
## Warning: Quick-TRANSfer stage steps exceeded maximum (= 3261000)
## Harmony 1/10
## Harmony 2/10
## Harmony 3/10
## Harmony 4/10
## Harmony converged after 4 iterations

Conventional integration removes variation associated with both batch and phenotype, yielding an embedding that primarily reflects the underlying cell states. This motivates our use of the Harmony embedding as a proxy for latent cell states.

Alternatively, (Z) could be estimated by directly fitting the latent variable model using maximum likelihood estimation; however, likelihood-based estimation of latent variable models is often computationally intensive and difficult to scale to large single-cell datasets. This strategy avoids costly model fitting and provides an efficient way to obtain an informative latent representation. For more details, please refer to our paper.

We store this representation in the Seurat object under the name estimate_z.

seurat_data[["estimate_z"]] <- CreateDimReducObject(
  embeddings = harmony_z,
  key = "estimatez_"
)
## Warning: No assay specified, setting assay as RNA by default.

The reduction name estimate_z is important because the current implementation of PhenoRec retrieves the estimated latent cell states from this reduction.

7 Encode batch and phenotype information

PhenoRec requires encoded matrices of categorical batch and phenotype variables. These are generated using encoding_function().

encoding_data <- encoding_function(
  seurat_data = seurat_data,
  batch_id = "donor_id",
  phenotype_id = "disease_state"
)

Here:

  • batch_id = "donor_id" specifies the batch variable;
  • phenotype_id = "disease_state" specifies the phenotype of interest.

For example, depending on the study design, the phenotype could represent:

  • disease status;
  • disease stage;
  • treatment condition;
  • longitudinal time point;
  • another biological condition of interest.

8 Prepare the input for PhenoRec

The PhenoRec implementation takes a list containing:

  1. the preprocessed Seurat object;
  2. the batch and phenotype encoding generated above.
input_data <- list(
  rna_data = seurat_data,
  encoding_data = encoding_data
)

9 Run PhenoRec

We now apply PhenoRec to the scRNA-seq data.

PhenoRec_result <- PhenoRec_normal(
  input = input_data
)
## PhenoRec completed.

In our implementation, normalized/scaled RNA measurements are modeled using Gaussian distribution.

The principal output for downstream analysis is:

integrated_data <- PhenoRec_result$integrated_data

integrated_data is the phenotype-preserving integrated data returned by PhenoRec. The integrated data can be directly used for visualization and downstream exploratory analyses.

10 Visualize the PhenoRec-integrated data

We place the PhenoRec-integrated matrix into a new Seurat object.

integrated_assay <- CreateAssayObject(
  data = t(integrated_data)
)

integrated_obj <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = integrated_assay,
  assay = "RNA",
  meta.data = seurat_data@meta.data
)
## Warning: Layer counts isn't present in the assay object; returning NULL
integrated_obj <- ScaleData(integrated_obj)
## Centering and scaling data matrix
## Warning: Layer counts isn't present in the assay object; returning NULL
integrated_obj <- RunPCA(
  integrated_obj,
  features = rownames(integrated_obj)
)

We again visualize the resulting UMAP according to cell type, donor, and phenotype.

DimPlot(
  integrated_obj,
  group.by = "cell_type_rename",
  label = TRUE
) +
  DimPlot(
    integrated_obj,
    group.by = "donor_id"
  ) +
  DimPlot(
    integrated_obj,
    group.by = "disease_state"
  )

The three plots provide complementary information about integration performance. The plots show that PhenoRec retained phenotype-associated structure, as reflected by clear separation between phenotype groups within specific cell types, indicating that the states of these cell populations differed across phenotype groups. For example, beta cells exhibited a pronounced cell-state shift between T1D and healthy controls.
